object.dateLabel: first shown 25 January 1896, Lyon; this print is the summer 1897 remake (Lumière catalogue no. 653)
object.medium: 35 mm silent film, about 50 seconds, shot with the Cinématographe Lumière
object.description: Fifty seconds, one fixed camera, no cut: a steam train pulls into the station at La Ciotat, on the coast east of Marseille where the Lumière family had a summer house, and passengers step down onto the platform. Louis Lumière set the Cinématographe at the platform's edge so that the locomotive grows from a speck to fill the frame and passes within arm's reach, a diagonal that still makes audiences lean back. The story that the first viewers fled screaming is a legend; the film was not even on the programme of the Lumières' first public show in Paris on 28 December 1895, and was first screened in Lyon in January 1896. It was popular enough that the brothers reshot it twice on the same platform; the version seen here, catalogue number 653, was taken in the summer of 1897 with Lumière children among the waiting passengers. The Cinématographe weighed five kilograms, was cranked by hand, and served as camera, printer and projector.
facts: Shown at about 16 frames a second from a reel of 17 metres: the length of one Lumière film.
Auguste and Louis Lumière ran their father's photographic-plate factory in Lyon; the camera was patented in February 1895.
By 1897 the Lumière catalogue listed over a thousand 'views' shot by operators across the world.
The film entered the public domain in France only on 1 January 2025, seventy years after Auguste Lumière's death.
